pulls.title: rpc: require a hex string for OP_RETURN data
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `createrawtransaction` accepts a JSON number as `data` when its digits form valid hex. For example, it treats `99` as the string `"99"` and writes the byte `0x99` to the output.

**Fix:** Pass the original JSON value to the hex parser so it can enforce the documented string type.

pulls.title: Improve loadtxoutset performance
pulls.body:
Significantly improves loadtxoutset performance via a number of changes:

 * parallel threads for decoding, hashing, serializing and writing to leveldb
 * no fsync() gating writes
 * no redundant loading into CoinsView
 
Also adds a subcommand to bitcoin-util for getting a snapshot's hash_serialized_3, muhash, coin count and total amount values without importing to leveldb first.

On my systems, performance ends up bottlenecked by leveldb CPU usage.

pulls.title: rpc: fix `getorphantxs` verbosity help and type checking
pulls.body:
**Problem:** #31043 removed the `verbose` alias from `getorphantxs`, but all three result headings in its help still use that name. Passing `verbose=1` as the help suggests returns `Unknown named parameter verbose`. The RPC also bypasses the schema’s numeric type check and reports a custom error for boolean inputs.

**Fix:** Use `verbosity` in all three result headings. Let the RPC schema check the argument type and supply its declared default of `0`. For boolean inputs, the RPC still returns error `-3`, now with the standard message identifying the argument by name and position.

pulls.title: rpc: generateblock to allow multiple outputs with custom payouts
pulls.body:
## Generatetomany

First approach was to create a `generatetomany` rpc call. That approach can be seen here https://github.com/polespinasa/bitcoin/pull/3

## Generateblock
Modifies `generateblock` to allow a user to set multiple outputs in the coinbase transaction. If an empty set is provided, the block will be empty. If no set of transactions is provided, the block will mine the mempool. If a set of transactions is provided only that set of txs will be mined.

```
$./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock bcrt1qw6qkj8wtw5hraxwxjp08m4aymkntms3yhqyacj
{
  "hash": "7359a3ed7af0f18f4016e6cb29193bd787a2452c584781135c585d5204b9ec5b"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]'
{
  "hash": "6db028454b26d6667dd6df45be2772844121fb44f86433f6bbfbafa429974684"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]' []

{
  "hash": "33e2ddc52546ddb0edf28bef5b295ee8fbd487b8aca19c97018467e2477877df"
}

```

### Motivation
https://x.com/SuperTestnet/status/1921220086645342550

Citating @supertestnet 
> When mining a block on regtest, the command "generatetoaddress" is available if you want to send the entire coinbase to 1 address. Let's add generatetomany in case you want to split up the coinbase among multiple addresses, similar to how the "sendtoaddress" and "sendmany" commands both exist and let you send money to (1) one address or (2) multiple addresses. The generatetomany command would be particularly useful for simulating protocols that send money to multiple recipients directly from a coinbase, as several pools do now, like ocean and braidpool.

pulls.title: log: mask SENSITIVE rw_settings in LogArgs
pulls.body:
`ArgsManager::LogArgs` masks `SENSITIVE` options from `bitcoin.conf` and the command line via `logArgsPrefix`, but prints `m_settings.rw_settings` values verbatim. Secrets such as `rpcpassword`, `rpcuser`, `rpcauth`, or `torpassword` stored in `settings.json` are therefore written in cleartext to `debug.log` and startup console output.

Resolve each `rw_settings` key with `InterpretKey` and mask its logged value with `****` when the registered option carries `ArgsManager::SENSITIVE`, while preserving existing logging for unknown settings.

Tests:
- `./build/bin/test_bitcoin --run_test=getarg_tests/logargs`
- `./build/test/functional/feature_settings.py`

pulls.title: validation: Ensure Invalid ValidationState has result
pulls.body:
Block and transaction validation results are represented in `ValidationState`, and invalid results in "Invalid" states. Invalid validation results have a `result`, an enum value, and a `reject_reason`, a structured string.

The change is to ensure that an __invalid result always has a set result and reject reason__. This increases code robustness/security.

One instance was identified where the result was not set, and is being fixed by a new `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result. PR #31981 moved a previous-block check from outside of `TestBlockValidity()` to inside it, and introduced a new usage of `BlockValidationState` with unset result. The result field is not checked outside. This instance is changed now to use the newly-introduced `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` value.

The new enum value is added to the kernel C API and its C++ wrapper. In P2P, a `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result does not lead to punishing the peer.

A few test-only instances with empty reject reason are changed to use a dummy value ("dummy-reason").

History: this was found on the side of #35570, but left untouched there; see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-5739477357 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#discussion_r4075379069.

Alternatives considered:

1. Use a new reject reason enum. This is the cleanest solution, but the cost is the extension of a widely-used validation enum.
2. Use a different mechanism for returning this specific case from `TestBlockValidity()`, e.g. using `util::Expected`, as you discussed. No need to touch the `BlockValidationResult` enum. However, in the call sites of `TestBlockValidity()`, the reject reason and debug strings are handled similarly to other non-valid check results, and they would need a special handling.
3. Reuse an exisiting reject reason enum value in `TestBlockValidity()`, with the comment "only in this spot it means a little different thing".
4. Create a special `TestBlockValidationResult`, "on top of" `BlockValidationResult`, with the extra value, and a special `TestBlockValidationState` (`ValidationState<TestBlockValidationResult>`). Use this in `TestBlockValidity()`. As this is used only internally, within this methods and at its call sites, the new value+state doesn't have to be exposed. Therefore the change has lower impact.

pulls.title: docs: sync external-signer.md with current external signer flow
pulls.body: Updated external-signer.md to match the current implementation. The signer network selection is passed as --chain rather than --testnet, and transaction signing is performed via stdin using the signtx command with JSON output containing a psbt field or error. Wallet creation for external signers requires external_signer=true with private keys disabled, so the example now uses named arguments. Spending with an external signer goes through the new send/sendall RPCs which build a PSBT, call the signer, and finalize when signatures are sufficient; sendtoaddress is not applicable for such wallets and also returns a plain txid for pk-enabled wallets rather than a complete field. The getdescriptors call is documented with the --account parameter and return shape including receive and internal arrays. Examples for displayaddress and createwallet are corrected, enumeratesigners now shows an optional name field, and references to bitcoin-qt replace the non-existent “bitcoin node” and “bitcoin rpc”.

Using `string_view` is easier and more compact than (as a previous version of this PR did) checking for trailing `\0`.

pulls.title: leveldb: correct trailer boundary check in Reader::SkipToInitialBlock
pulls.body:
replaces the magic number 6 in the trailer boundary condition with kHeaderSize and corrects an off-by-one by expressing the rule as offset_in_block > kBlockSize - kHeaderSize, which is equivalent to offset_in_block >= kBlockSize - 6. According to 
src/leveldb/doc/log_format.md:
“A record never starts within the last six bytes of a block” 
and when exactly seven bytes remain a record may start (e.g., a zero-length FIRST), so the equal case must be treated as trailer. The writer already uses kHeaderSize to manage trailers, and aligning the reader with kHeaderSize removes a format-coupled magic number and ensures future-proof consistency. Functionally this avoids scanning a block when initial_offset_ is in the last six bytes, matching the documented format; it was previously a minor inefficiency and comment mismatch rather than a correctness issue.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: [RFC] ipc: add Events interface for chain and mempool notifications
pulls.body:
This adds an Events IPC interface that streams block and mempool events in one ordered stream, addressing gaps in ZMQ notifications and providing a more modular interface. It supports the following subscriptions:

- `blockConnected`: fires for every block connected to the active chain, including during IBD (blocks connected by a background assumeutxo chainstate are skipped). Carries hash, height and optionally the serialized block. ZMQ `hashblock`/`rawblock` are driven by UpdatedBlockTip, so they skip intermediate blocks when several connect at once and don't fire during IBD.
- `blockDisconnected`: fires for every block disconnected during a reorg, with hash, height and optionally the serialized block.
- `txAddedToMempool`: fires only for mempool acceptance. Carries txid, wtxid, mempool sequence, fee, vsize and optionally the serialized tx. ZMQ `hashtx`/`rawtx` also fire for every tx in connected and disconnected blocks, so a subscriber can't tell whether a tx entered the mempool (pain point of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/19462#issuecomment-658304417, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23624#issue-1065790580 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/7753).
- `txRemovedFromMempool`: fires for every removal, including txs removed because they were mined (reason `block`), except during IBD, with txid, wtxid, mempool sequence, removal reason and optionally the serialized tx.

ZMQ `sequence` covers all four of these, but only carries hashes (plus the mempool sequence for "A"/"R"), and "R" doesn't include block-inclusion removals or a reason.

Why not just do it with ZMQ?

- One ordered stream that includes the data. `rawblock`/`rawtx` have their own sequence numbers and can't be ordered against `sequence`. Here every event can include its serialized block or tx in the same ordered stream. Events come in the same order as ZMQ `sequence`, plus block-inclusion removals.
- Typed, versioned interface. Cap'n Proto generates the client code and lets the schema [evolve without breaking older clients](https://capnproto.org/language.html#evolving-your-protocol). With ZMQ, clients parse raw bytes by hand which can't evolve existing topics without breaking changes.
- Fixing these in ZMQ would need new topics reporting on the same events as existing ones, which is confusing for users, and changing the existing topics would break current consumers.
- Bounded buffering. Events are buffered per subscription up to a byte limit (`-ipceventsbuffer`), and the client pulls them in batches with waitNext. ZMQ limits are message counts per topic (-zmqpub*hwm), which don't bound memory when messages are full blocks.

Why additional data, including derivable ones?

- fee, vsize: neither can be derived from the tx alone, so including them saves RPC calls per tx. RPC calls can also fail if the tx was removed in the time in between.
- mempool sequence: lets a client line events up with `getrawmempool` (`mempool_sequence=true`) to bootstrap and keep a mempool mirror in sync.
- height: not in the serialized block, and needed to handle reorgs without an extra RPC call.
- hash, txid, wtxid: identifiers are always included, so clients don't need to branch on `include_data`.

Example of simple clients using this interface, including a mempool mirror: https://github.com/ViniciusCestarii/bitcoin-ipc-events-client

Note: to make this interface usable in this PR, the Cap'n Proto `union` that this uses is mapped by hand in `events-types.h`. Ideally this support would be added to libmultiprocess first.

pulls.title: rpc, wallet: Convert walletprocesspsbt to use options parameter
pulls.body:
This picks up #24963.

`walletprocesspsbt` takes four settings after the PSBT, three of them booleans, so a positional call reads `walletprocesspsbt "psbt" true "ALL" true false`, and each new setting becomes one more positional parameter (#32857 would add a sixth). - A null option means the default, as a null named argument does on master.
- From review on #24963, the options are checked before the wallet sync and the PSBT decode, and a test mixes positional and named arguments.
- Unit tests for the framework changes.

pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. The tests and documentation have since been improved, but the consensus-critical commits have been carried over with only minor differences (the only behavioural one being the addition of the stripped-size check to `PreChecks`).

Roughly 95% of the added lines are tests or test data. The format, contents, and reproduction procedure for the BIP 54 test vectors are documented [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/tree/master/bip-0054/test_vectors). The `bip54_tests` unit test module exercises each mitigation extensively in isolation. The `feature_bip54.py` functional test verifies all of them end-to-end after and prior to activation. For the timestamp rules, it simulates timewarp and Murch–Zawy attacks, demonstrating the new timestamp rules prevent these exploits. A fuzz harness for the sigop accounting logic is also included, which can be seeded from the BIP test vectors (implemented [here](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/bip54_seed_fuzz_corpus)).

See commit messages for details.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: mining: avoid checkBlock crash when chain has no tip
pulls.body:
**The problem**: `Init.makeMining` returns as soon as the chainstate is loaded. On a first start with an empty datadir, or on a node started with `-reindex`/`-reindex-chainstate`, this is before the genesis block is connected, so the active chain has no tip. A `Mining.checkBlock` call in this window reaches `TestBlockValidity()`, which asserts that the tip exists, and the node aborts.

**The fix**: in `MakeMining`, if `wait_loaded` is set, wait for the chainstate to be present and for the tip to be non-null. 

*Alternative fix*: In `Mining.checkBlock`, check if the tip is present, return early with "inconclusive-no-chain-tip" otherwise. (I initially implemented this fix, but decided to go with the `makeMining` one instead, see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36908#discussion_r4610682758)

The crash can be reproduced on master using the functional test included in this PR.

This is joint work with Turtlecute33 :)

pulls.title: Enhanced error messages for invalid network prefix during address parsing.
pulls.body:
# Improve Address Decoding Error Messages

Fixes #26290.

## Issue

`DecodeDestination` gives misleading errors when a user inputs a valid address for the wrong network (e.g. a signet address while running on mainnet). Because the Bech32-vs-Base58 dispatch guessed the encoding from the address prefix, a valid Bech32 address for a different network fell through to the Base58 path and reported "Invalid or unsupported Segwit (Bech32) or Base58 encoding."

## Approach

- **Decode first, then validate**: the input is decoded with `bech32::Decode()` upfront (on a lowercased copy, so mixed-case input can be diagnosed explicitly without decoding twice) instead of prefix-guessing. Valid Bech32 addresses for other networks now reach the HRP check and report the expected and actual prefix. Malformed input is diagnosed by the most specific applicable decoder.
- **Separated helpers**: `DecodeDestination` is split into `DecodeBech32Destination()` / `DecodeBase58Destination()`; pure moves/refactors are in their own commits, separate from behavior changes.
- **Structured Bech32 errors**: `bech32::LocateErrors()` now returns a `bech32::Error` code plus locations instead of a message string; `key_io` maps codes to user-facing messages via `Bech32ErrorMessage()`.
- **Network-aware Base58 errors**: expected human-readable prefixes (e.g. "1", "3") come from a new `CChainParams::Base58PrefixText()` table populated for every network and `Base58Type`.

## Error message changes

| Scenario | Previous | New |
|----------|----------|-----|
| Bech32 address for another network | "Invalid or unsupported Segwit (Bech32) or Base58 encoding." | "Invalid or unsupported prefix for Segwit (Bech32) address (expected bc, got tb)" |
| Mixed-case Bech32 string | "Invalid character or mixed case" | "Bech32 address is mixed case" (with offending character positions) |
| Bech32 checksum/format errors | bare message from `LocateErrors` | "Bech32 address decoded with error: …" |
| Base58 address with another network's version bytes | "Invalid or unsupported Base58-encoded address." | "Invalid Base58 address. Expected prefix 3 or 1" |
| Base58 checksum/length failure | "Invalid or unsupported Segwit (Bech32) or Base58 encoding." | "Invalid checksum or length of Base58 address (P2PKH or P2SH)" |
| Input that is neither | "Invalid or unsupported Segwit (Bech32) or Base58 encoding." | "Address is not valid Base58 or Bech32" |

Consistency: the trailing period was dropped from the wrong-network prefix message, and the witness program size error now says "SegWit v0" instead of "Bech32 v0" (the version is a SegWit concept, not an encoding one).

## Tests

- `test/functional/data/rpc_validateaddress.json`: new data file with test vectors keyed by network; `rpc_validateaddress.py` runs them on both signet and mainnet (restarting the node in between), re-enabling the `tb1` BIP 173/350 vectors that were commented out in #27727 and dropping duplicates.
- `rpc_invalid_address_message.py` and `wallet_basic.py` updated for the new messages.
- New `key_io` unit test checking `Base58PrefixText()` on all networks; `bech32` unit tests updated for the error-code enum.

**Problem:** If the node is stopped while `importdescriptors` is rescanning, the call still returns success for descriptors whose history was not scanned. The wallet's best block is already at the tip, so nothing rescans on the next start, and the transactions stay missing until a manual `rescanblockchain`.

**Fix:** Treat a rescan that shutdown cut short like one stopped with `abortrescan`: the import fails with the existing "Rescan aborted by user." error. In both cases the descriptors stay in the wallet.

pulls.title: contrib: require trusted signers in verify.py
pulls.body:
`verify_shasums_signature` previously separated signatures into `good_trusted` and `good_untrusted`, but computed `num_trusted = len(good_trusted) + len(good_untrusted)` (and added all `expired` entries under `--allow-expired`). As a result, valid signatures from untrusted keys present in the local GPG keyring satisfied `--min-good-sigs` even when none of them were trusted in GPG or matched `--trusted-keys`.

In addition, `README.md` documents passing full 40-character primary key fingerprints to `--trusted-keys`, whereas `parse_gpg_result` only recorded the key identifier from `GOODSIG`/`EXPKEYSIG` and ignored `VALIDSIG` fingerprints, and did not deduplicate multiple signatures from the same primary key.

Changes:
- Count only distinct, non-revoked trusted signers toward `--min-good-sigs` (including under `--allow-expired`) directly in the signature loop.
- Parse signing and primary key fingerprints from GnuPG `VALIDSIG` status lines so `--trusted-keys` matches full fingerprints while deduplicating by primary key fingerprint.
- Clarify `--trusted-keys` and signer counting in `contrib/verify-binaries/README.md`.
- Extend `test_inactive_signature_quorum` in `contrib/verify-binaries/test.py`.

pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.

pulls.title: Add util::ResultPtr class
pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #25665.** The non-base commits are:

- [`3d008913cdb` Add util::ResultPtr class](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/3d008913cdb697651e67cd5ee158cc12a9611c0e)
- [`2d0915656c8` Use ResultPtr<unique_ptr> instead of Result<unique_ptr>](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/2d0915656c80d45642965b1963f158d865846f5b)<!-- end -->

---

The `util::ResultPtr` class is a wrapper for `util::Result` providing syntax sugar to make it less awkward to use with returned pointers. Instead of needing to be deferenced twice with `**result` or `(*result)->member`, it only needs to be dereferenced once with `*result` or `result->member`. Also when it is used in a boolean context, instead of evaluating to true when there is no error and the pointer is null, it evaluates to false so it is straightforward to determine whether the result points to something.

This PR is only partial a solution to #26004 because while it makes it easier to check for null pointer values, it does not make it impossible to return a null pointer value inside a successful result. It would be possible to enforce that successful results always contain non-null pointers by using a `not_null` type (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/24423) in combination with `ResultPtr`, though.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: script: prevent partial reinitialization of sighash data
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `PrecomputedTransactionData` could be default-constructed and filled later with `Init()`.
That allowed an object to exist without transaction-specific data and left a public reuse path that was easy to get wrong.
The old `Init()` guard only checked [`m_spent_outputs_ready`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/2063f02bd5edebe1b5c9635db8850220811ebc90/src/script/interpreter.cpp#L1415), which remained false after initialization without spent outputs even when the BIP143 prevout, sequence, and output hashes were already cached.
No current caller reuses an object across transactions, so validation and signing results are unchanged.
`btck_script_pubkey_verify()` in the experimental kernel C API also copied caller-supplied txdata on each verification call.

**Fix:** Remove default construction and `Init()` so each `PrecomputedTransactionData` object is built for one transaction.
Callers that already have the transaction and optional spent outputs construct it directly.
Validation stores txdata in `std::optional` and emplaces it only after a script-cache miss, keeping precomputation lazy.
`ConnectBlock()` also leaves txdata storage empty when assumevalid skips script checks, covering #35663.
The kernel verification path binds directly to caller-supplied txdata and constructs a local fallback only when needed.

pulls.title: script: clarify implicit signature-cache input requirements
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Signature-cache hashing relies on input requirements that are implicit at its public entry methods.
Inspired by the Elements rangeproof-cache vulnerability behind the recent [Liquid incident](https://blog.blockstream.com/liquid-network-security-incident-assessment) and the [subsequent cache-key fix](https://github.com/ElementsProject/elements/pull/1600), this change clarifies an easy-to-misread hashing pattern: `Write(data, size)` hashes the data bytes without encoding the size.
Bitcoin Core's cache keys already include the signature hash, public key, and signature in separate ECDSA and Schnorr domains.
Bitcoin Core's signature-cache encoding is unambiguous for inputs accepted by its current script checker: a valid ECDSA public key's prefix determines its length, while a Schnorr public key is always 32 bytes, leaving the signature as the remaining suffix.

**Fix:** Use native `HashWriter` serialization in the typed `ComputeEntry*` methods so ECDSA public keys and signature vectors include their CompactSize lengths.
Schnorr retains its fixed-size public-key encoding and raw signature span.
Return the digest by value from the public `ComputeEntry*` methods so callers explicitly initialize the cache entry, where the previous chained `Finalize(entry.begin())` obscured the output assignment.
Keep the prepared salt prefixes private and const, and copy them locally for each entry.
Retain the ECDSA salt padding and drop the Schnorr salt padding.
Add a nonce-taking constructor so tests can reproduce the encoding deterministically.
The process-local cache-entry bytes change, while script validity rules are unchanged.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** To send a `MSG_BLOCK` reply from disk, a node currently decodes the block and serializes it again without witnesses.
For `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK`, it already sends the stored bytes directly.
Serving `MSG_BLOCK` efficiently also matters for the proposed witnessless initial block download. [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476)

**Fix:** For `MSG_BLOCK` replies from disk on non-Signet chains, read the block into an owned byte buffer and check the header’s proof of work and expected hash.
Walk the serialized transactions directly and strip their witnesses in place.
Signet still uses `ReadBlock` to verify the Signet solution.
Header checks now run before transaction parsing, so if both the header and transaction data are corrupt, the node may log a different error.

**Performance:**
| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 3.204 ms | 0.369 ms | **8.7×** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 8.944 ms | 1.026 ms | **8.7×** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the path that sends witness blocks directly from disk. [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151)
Earlier work identified unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) · [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098)
The implementation also builds on bulk block reads. [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551)

pulls.title: blockstorage: fix partial-mask assertions and genesis availability checks
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `CheckBlockDataAvailability` checks whether the upper block has any requested bit. `GetFirstBlock` requires every requested bit, so a partial match can reach its assertion. At genesis, the existing undo exception can reject an undo-only request or accept a request with missing block data. It also misses ranges containing only genesis.

**Fix:** Require every requested bit on each block in the range, except that genesis needs no undo data. An empty mask now succeeds for a valid range because it requests no bits. Both index-startup calls supply nonempty masks.

pulls.title: log, refactor: Allow log macros to accept context arguments
pulls.body:
Allow `LogTrace()`, `LogDebug()`, `LogInfo()`, `LogWarning()`, and `LogError()` macros to accept context arguments to provide more information in log messages and more control over logging to callers.

For example, with this change wallet code can log with (in #30343):

```diff
-        WalletLogPrintf("Error: cannot erase address book entry data\n");
+        LogError(m_log, "Error: cannot erase address book entry data\n");
```

And kernel code can log with (in #30342):

```diff
-        LogDebug(BCLog::VALIDATION, "Block mutated: %s\n", state.ToString());
+        LogDebug(log, "Block mutated: %s\n", state.ToString());
```

where `m_log` / `log` types can vary and be defined by the subsystem. This allows subsystems to attach extra context to log messages like wallet names, or request ids. It also allows more than a single log stream to exist, and for messages to be logged to specified streams. Having a single global log stream works very well for `bitcoind` and will not change. But it limits functionality of libbitcoinkernel, forcing all potential users of the library, including applications written in different languages and running in different environments (like jupyter notebooks) to use shared global state and not be able to do things like get an isolated log trace from one operation.

The change is fully backwards compatible and does not require any updates to code that wants to continue using the macros as they are. The implementation of the macros is also improved. They now provide improved error messages when called with the wrong arguments. And they only call underlying `ShouldLog` `Log` and `Format` hooks as needed to avoid unnecessary work. The PR also adds more test coverage and documentation.

---

Note: Originally this PR also removed some restrictions around passing category constants to log macros to try to make them more consistent, but these changes were too controversial and have been dropped.

---

pulls.title: mining: handle negative and NaN wait timeouts
pulls.body:
An ipc client can pass any timeout to `waitTipChanged`, but the code assumes it is never negative:

```
Assume(timeout >= 0ms); // No internal callers should use a negative timeout
```

On debug builds, a negative or NaN timeout fails this check and aborts the node. I reproduced this with a timeout of -1.0.

On release builds the check is skipped. Negative values are clamped to zero, but NaN is not, because every comparison with NaN is false. It ends up as the deadline passed to `wait_until`.

`waitNext` has no Assume, but it also doesn't check its timeout. A NaN timeout waits one extra fee tick (about one second) before returning.

`waitTipChanged` and `waitNext` now throw an error for negative or NaN timeouts. The internal `Assume` in `WaitTipChanged` still checks internal callers. The interface documents the errors, and the functional test covers rejection of negative and NaN timeouts and acceptance of positive infinity in both methods.

I'm not aware of any client that sends these values (sv2-tp, for example, requires an interval of at least one second), so this is hardening against bad input from ipc clients.

_This is similar to #36520, which handles invalid arguments to the Chain interface for the same reason._

Links

- https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/bugs/bitcoin-2026-wait-timeout-assume/

pulls.title: mining: add getMemoryLoad() and track template non-mempool memory footprint
pulls.body:
IPC clients can hold block templates indefinitely, keeping transactions alive after they leave the mempool. This adds `getMemoryLoad()` to estimate the memory held on behalf of all mining clients, as discussed in bitcoin/bitcoin#33899. It does not impose a limit.

The estimate includes each tracked template's vectors and the transactions it references that are no longer in the mempool. Transaction objects shared by multiple templates are counted once. Dummy coinbase transactions and the template cached by the `getblocktemplate` RPC are excluded.

`BlockTemplateManager` tracks templates through weak references, so the registry does not prolong their lifetime. Templates unregister when destroyed, including when IPC cleanup happens after shutdown has reset the manager. Clients can reduce the reported memory load by releasing stale templates or explicitly calling `destroy()`.

The result is an estimate: the mempool can change during calculation, and eviction followed by re-entry as a different transaction object can cause undercounting.

Example client usage: [stratum-mining/sv2-tp#63](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp/pull/63).

Commits:

- `refactor: share ownership of BlockTemplateManager`
- `mining: track block templates held by IPC clients`
- `mining: add GetTemplateMemoryUsage()`
- `ipc: add getMemoryLoad()`
- `test: check template memory accounting invariants`

pulls.body:
Since #36895, `btck_witness_stack_get_item_at` walks the items before the one it returns, so reading a whole witness stack through it is O(n^2).

This keeps a span for each item in `btck_WitnessStack`, which makes `btck_witness_stack_get_item_at` O(1) without changing its signature. `btck_transaction_input_get_witness_stack` is O(n) instead of O(1), because it finds every item when it creates the witness stack.

Breaking changes:
- `btck_transaction_input_get_witness_stack` returns an owned `btck_WitnessStack*`, which must be destroyed with `btck_witness_stack_destroy`.
- The C++ wrapper's `WitnessStackView` is removed, and `GetWitnessStack()` returns a `WitnessStack`.

pulls.title: CAT in Tapscript (BIP-347)
pulls.body:
# CAT in Tapscript

This PR provides the necessary code to enable the opcode OP\_CAT in Tapscript as specified in [BIP-347: OP\_CAT in Tapscript](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) and [BIN-2024-0001](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/binana/blob/master/2024/BIN-2024-0001.md),

**Important:** This PR *does not* include miner activation functionality. This means that merging this PR into bitcoin-core will not make OP\_CAT functional in Bitcoin.
If this PR is merged it is *not* a signal of community consensus around activating CAT nor be read as a portent about the activation process or timeline.
The PR is not a stand-in for consensus around such decisions.

This PR includes:

- An implementation of the Tapscript opcode OP\_CAT along with the flags `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` and `SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT`.
- Integration and unit tests which ensure that our CAT  implementation works as expected. This includes ensuring that CAT never uses more that 520 bytes of stack memory. A full description of what these tests cover is given below.
- An improvement to `src/test/script_tests.cpp` JSON script format enabling the rapid creation of new Tapscript unit tests.

## Activation on Bitcoin-inquisition (signet)

[Bitcoin-inquisition PR 37](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39) which contained our implementation of OP\_CAT [was merged into bitcoin-inquisition (signet) on Apr 25 2024](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39), released as [bitcoin-inquisition release 25.2 on Apr 26 2024.](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/releases/tag/v25.2-inq) and activated in bitcoin-inquisition Apr 30 2024. The bitcoin-inquisition PR was reviewed in the PR review club [(transcript of discussion)](https://bitcoincore.reviews/bitcoin-inquisition-39). Since Apr 30 2024 there have been many OP\_CAT transactions created and spent on signet.

The code merged into bitcoin-inquisition differs from this PR, as we have removed the consensus logic which was used to activate it on signet.

## OP\_CAT Tapscript Implementation

We implement OP\_CAT as a new Tapscript op code by redefining the opcode OP\_SUCCESS126 (126 in decimal and 0x7e in hexadecimal). This is the same opcode value used by the original OP_CAT.

When evaluated, the OP\_CAT instruction:

1. Pops the top two values off the stack,
2. concatenates the popped values together in stack order,
3. and then pushes the concatenated value on the top of the stack.

OP\_CAT fails if there are fewer than two values on the stack or if a concatenated value would have a combined size greater than the maximum script element size of 520 bytes.

See [BIP 347](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) for a deeper description.

### Errors thrown

If evaluated OP\_CAT can throw the following errors:

- If at time of evaluation the stack has fewer than two elements we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_INVALID_STACK_OPERATION`
- If at time of evaluation the top two stack elements have a combined size greater than `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE` (520 bytes) we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`.

### Script verification flags

While this PR does not contain any miner signaling and activation logic and can not activate OP\_CAT, it does contain two flags which future activation logic could set to control activation of OP\_CAT.

- `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` IF a bitcoin node has this set to true, then it treat OP\_CAT enabled for Tapscript. That is, OP\_SUCCESS126 will be redefining to OP\_CAT in Tapscript. If this was set to true at the consensus level this would cause a soft fork.

`SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` When set to true, a node receiving any Tapscript transaction containing the opcode OP\_CAT or OP\_SUCCESS126 will reject the transaction throwing the error `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` but not banning the node which relayed the transaction. This prevents nodes from relaying transactions with OP\_CAT. This  is equivalent to the behavior of `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT = true` when `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT = false` as OP\_CAT is an OP\_SUCCESS (OP\_SUCCESS126).

This is how these two flags are intended to be used to ensure a smooth soft fork.

| Stage | `SCRIPT_VERIFY OP_CAT` | `SCRIPT_VERIFY DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1.Default** | False | True | This does not represent any change in behavior of the bitcoin-core node. |
| **2.Upgrading** | True | True | OP\_CAT is activating. |
| **3.Upgraded** | True | False | It is clear that OP\_CAT has been activated and the network has been upgraded. |

The flag `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` provides a window of time for the network to fully activate, before nodes will relay or accept transactions containing OP\_CAT in their mem pools.

## Tests

This PR contains a suite of script tests to ensure that OP\_CAT functions as expected. In the JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`), we test:

- That if OP\_CAT is not activated that there are no changes to bitcoin consensus.
- That regardless of the activation or non-activation of OP\_CAT in Tapscript, pre-Tapscript scripts, i.e. Bitcoin scripts, have no changes in behavior.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated throws the expected error when there are less than two elements on the stack.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated in a variety of circumstances and edge cases, successfully concatenates elements of the stack. This includes:
  - multiple calls to OP\_CAT in a row,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT inside of a IF conditional,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on zero size stack elements, random and large stack elements,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on values being moved to and from the alt stack,
  - and checking that when evaluated OP\_CAT concatenates the elements in the expected order.

All of these tests are designed to cover the happy path of OP\_CAT, the various errors which OP\_CAT can throw and all the corner cases between those two outcomes.

Additionally we include three tests outside of the JSON script tests.

- `cat_simple` and `cat_empty_stack` are designed to test OP\_CAT outside of the JSON serialization regime. Ensure that we catch bugs that we might miss in the JSON script tests due to a bug introduced at the JSON serialization layer.
- `cat_dup_test` enumerates all stack element sizes from 1 to 522 bytes and then enumerates up to 10 repetitions of `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT`. It then tests if the stack element would exceed 520 bytes and if so did OP\_CAT throw the error `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`. This allows us to be certain that OP\_CAT will not introduce any `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT` memory exhaustion attacks.

### Better Tapscript tests in JSON script tests

While writing these JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`) we ran into the following problem. The JSON script tests are simple and easy to write for pre-Tapscript scripts, but adding or changing a Tapscript test requires substantial work per test.
Consider the following pre-tapscript test:

```json
["'aa' 'bb'", "CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL", "P2SH,STRICTENC", "DISABLED_OPCODE", "CAT disabled"]
```

whereas a Tapscript test for the same script (annotated with comments for better readability) would look like:

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "7e4c02aabb87", // output script
        "c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d", // control block
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99", // Tapscript output
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT CATs aa and bb together and checks if EQUAL to aabb"
]
```

Computing the Tapscript output, such as `0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99`, requires writing custom code and running it for each test. The same is true for the Tapscript control block, such as `c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d`. If a test is changed or updated new outputs and control blocks must be computed. The complexity of doing this is likely the reason that no one has added any Tapscript tests to JSON script tests until this PR.

In this PR we address this issue by adding the following improvements to JSON script tests:

- Adding simple macros (`"#SCRIPT#` and `#CONTROLBLOCK#`) that allow the script test parser to automatically generate and inject a valid Tapscript output and control block to be computed automatically from the JSON script.
- Allowing Tapscript scripts to use the human readable strings like pre-script scripts by marking the location of the script in the witness stack using `#SCRIPT#`. This transforms the unreadable script `7e4c02aabb87` into `#SCRIPT# CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL`.

This results in the following JSON script test which is far easier to write and easier to read.

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "#SCRIPT# CAT",
        "#CONTROLBLOCK#",
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 #TAPROOTOUTPUT#",
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT,OP_CAT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT Test of OP_CAT flag by calling CAT on two elements. TAPSCRIPT_OP_CAT flag is set so CAT is executed."
],
```

pulls.title: headersync: do parameter search at runtime
pulls.body:
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime whenever a headers sync starts. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000 if they want to maintain the attack. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.

pulls.title: mining: add TxCollection to bandwidth-efficiently validate external block templates
pulls.body:
The Stratum v2 spec defines a [Job Declarator Server](https://stratumprotocol.org/specification/06-job-declaration-protocol) (JDS), whose job it is to approve custom miner templates. Since #34020 it can use `getTransactionsByWitnessID()` to request transactions from the node, instead of maintaining its own mempool mirror (see https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/pull/911), and then request any missing transactions from the miner.

The new `TxCollection` interface introduced by this PR optimizes this further. We build and validate the block template ourselves now, based on the requested transaction list and our own mempool, so known transactions don't need to cross the IPC boundary. This also fits the [draft spec](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-spec/discussions/239) for JDS custom job validation through a Template Provider.

The following flow is demonstrated in https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/pull/599:

1. Miner generates a template, e.g. using our `createNewBlock()` IPC method
2. They send the list of `Wtxid`s to the pool's JDS
3. JDS calls `Mining::collectTxs()` (this PR) with that `Wtxid` list
4. We check the list against our mempool and hold a `CTransactionRef` for each match
5. The JDS queries `unknownTxPos()` to learn what's missing from the collection
6. The JDS requests the fully serialized missing transactions from the miner (using native Stratum v2 messages)
7. JDS calls `addMissingTxs()` which completes the collection
8. JDS calls `makeTemplate()` which reconstructs the block and validates it, optionally with the coinbase it intends to use (e.g. to check the reward amount); a node-generated dummy is used otherwise. The JDS needs the check to succeed, may relay the BIP-22 failure reason to the miner.
9. It returns a `BlockTemplate` which works as if we generated the template ourselves, but with methods like `waitNext()` disabled. The JDS can call `submitSolution()` (the sv2 spec allows for redundant block reconstruction by both the miner node and the JDS).

If this sounds very similar to compact block relay: it is! In fact, it would be easy to expand the above methods to take transaction short ids instead of `Wtxid`. That may be useful for the [p2pool revival project](https://www.vinteum.org/blog/reviving-p2pool-welcoming-johnny-santos-as-a-vinteum-grantee), which needs a way to validate and relay weak blocks as compact blocks. The p2pool client software would need to (trivially) verify the PoW, but could use the `TxCollection` interface to reconstruct and verify the block content. That said, the SRI [JDS](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20JDS) implementation is much further along and likely to be the first consumer of this.

Commits:

- _ipc: add TxCollection scaffold_ - step 3 and 4
- _mining: add TxCollection unknownTxPos_ - step 5
- _mining: add TxCollection addMissingTxs_ - step 7
- _mining: add coinbase transaction helper_ - we need a dummy coinbase to verify the block, so extract a helper from `BlockAssembler::CreateNewBlock()`
- _mining: assemble block templates from TxCollection_ - step 8, node implementation
- _ipc: expose TxCollection template creation_ - step 8 and 9, including restrictions on externally generated templates
- _mining: allow TxCollection templates to use a supplied coinbase_ - optional coinbase in step 8

Potential followups:

- https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/122
- expose total fees for externally generated templates, building on #36525
- have `addMissingTxs()` (optionally) insert favorable transactions into our mempool
- add a data structure to store transactions that don't meet our mempool threshold (so `TxCollection` can grab them, instead of needing another round trip)
