pulls.title: policy: make unstructured Taproot annexes standard
pulls.body:
Make Taproot annexes standard for key and script paths:

- `0x50`: marker-only opt-in.
- `0x50 0x00 <data>`: arbitrary data; other prefixes remain nonstandard.
- All non-P2A inputs must carry an annex, or none may. P2A witnesses must be empty.

No annex-specific size limit; the existing 400,000 WU standard transaction limit applies.

This opt-in rule protects transactions that do not opt in. It does not prevent annex inflation by opted-in participants. Consensus and witness replacement are unchanged.

Builds on #27926 and [Libre Relay](https://github.com/petertodd/bitcoin/commit/04c8e449a34e74e048bf5751d13592a22763ff7e).

Validation: full build, 17 transaction unit tests, full `feature_taproot.py`, and `git diff --check` passed.

AI-assisted implementation and tests.

pulls.title: bip352: match P2SH-P2WPKH instead of evaluating it
pulls.body:
For P2SH inputs, `GetPubKeyFromInput` evaluated the full scriptSig with `EvalScript` and then ran `Solver` on the redeem script, even though only P2SH-P2WPKH is eligible for BIP-352. That costs time on every non-segwit P2SH spend (e.g. multisig), whose scriptSigs can be up to `MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE`.

BIP-141 requires the scriptSig of a P2SH-wrapped witness program to be exactly a single push of the redeem script (`SCRIPT_ERR_WITNESS_MALLEATED_P2SH`). So any valid P2SH-P2WPKH scriptSig is exactly `0x16 OP_0 0x14 <20-byte keyhash>`, and matching that template gives the same result without evaluating anything.

### Benchmarks

`bench_bitcoin -filter='BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_.*' -min-time=2000`, Release build.

Before:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|              688.30 |        1,452,858.07 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            7,158.19 |          139,700.11 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

After:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|               56.87 |       17,584,611.40 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            6,949.45 |          143,896.18 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

P2SH multisig is about 12x faster to rule out. P2SH-P2WPKH saves about 200 ns per input; its time is still dominated by `CPubKey::IsFullyValid()`.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: net, http: handle socket errors separately from reads
pulls.body:
On Linux a socket error or hangup is reported whether or not we asked for it. If that happens for a peer we did not request to read from, disconnect directly. This just adds clarity: previously we would attempt a send that would then fail. The only side-effect is a changed log message. Nothing changes on other platforms: since bitcoin/bitcoin#36716 they no longer report errors for established connections.

The last commit does the same for HTTP, where on error it also no longer attempts a final read from a client whose reads are paused.

As a followup to bitcoin/bitcoin#36716, `p2p_socket_errors.py` adds coverage for existing behavior:
- the node ignores a single urgent byte: the connection stays open, ordinary data is still processed and the urgent byte is not counted as received.
- a peer resets the connection while the node's send to it is stalled and receiving from it is paused: the node disconnects without reading anything more (the change above only changes the log message)

Similarly `interface_http.py` checks that:
- a single urgent byte does not disturb an ordinary request.
- a client reset while the server has unsent responses (the HTTP change only changes the log message)

The first commit drops a comment from the `wait_ignores_urgent_data` unit test, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#discussion_r4700726004.

To support the new tests, the test framework gains:
- `wait_for_send_stall()`, moved out of `p2p_ping_ibd.py`
- a `reset` option for `peer_disconnect()`, which closes the connection with a TCP reset
- `mine_large_block()` returns the block hash and size
- `pack_linger()`, and `linux_host` / `windows_target` to tell which log message to expect

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

`CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. A follow-up #36918 with optimizations improves the worst case deserialization time significantly instead. Other minor degradations:
* libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
* `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: net: only monitor select exceptions while connecting
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
>
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by only adding a socket to the `select()` exception set while waiting for a non-blocking `connect()` to complete. Windows needs that to detect a failed connection. Established connections no longer monitor the exception set on any platform. This approach was suggested by theuni in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#issuecomment-6931290348.

To opt in, `ErrorEvent` can now be requested from `Sock::Wait()`, like `RecvEvent` and `SendEvent`. With `select()` that adds the socket to the exception set. `ConnectToSocket()` is the only caller that requests it. There is no behavior change with `poll()`, which reports errors whether or not they are requested. Using `ErrorEvent` for this was suggested by vasild in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#discussion_r4692637894.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

A new unit test in `sock_tests` covers the fix itself: with an urgent byte pending, waiting for `RecvEvent` must not report `ErrorEvent`. Without the fix it fails on a `select()` build.

Backports until 29.x are straight-forward, but for 31.x and before require compensating for the scripted-diff in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/f395acdeeeaa1f3fd75d3cedbf2731fa24083e9f.

pulls.title: test: cover compact blocks far ahead of the tip
pulls.body:
This adds a test that passes on master and fails with the diff from #34618 applied, as davidgumberg asked in #34722. It covers both things that diff removes for a compact block more than two blocks ahead of the tip.

If the node already requested the block from this peer, it sends another `getdata` for the full block. Without that `getdata`, the block stays in flight from this peer and nothing requests it again until the block download timeout disconnects the peer. This check is the one shuv-amp proposed in #34722.

Otherwise, from a high-bandwidth peer, the node handles the header as a headers message (`fRevertToHeaderProcessing`). Most of that work is done anyway. As 151henry151 pointed out in #34618, one part is not: protecting an outbound peer from eviction (`m_chain_sync.m_protect`). The test checks for the "Protecting outbound peer" debug log line.

Each check fails when only its branch is disabled: `fRevertToHeaderProcessing = false` fails the protection check, and `if (false)` in place of `if (requested_block_from_this_peer)` makes the `getdata` check time out. shuv-amp first tested the two branches separately in #34618.

Fixes #34618.

*Made with my usual tools: a computer, the Internet and an LLM. The mistakes, as usual, are all mine.*

pulls.title: descriptor: Expose key expression parsing
pulls.body:
This PR exposes a utility function to parse and validate a standalone descriptor key expression. 
This is particularly useful in GUI multisig setup flows where the UI accepts a pasted key expression. The GUI can use this parser to validate input, inspect the parsed key,  and apply setup-specific policy i.e. reject private keys, uncompressed keys etc. (Multisig Wizard tracking issue: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35645)

`PubkeyProvider` is the existing internal representation of a parsed key expression. This PR exposes its interface in `descriptor.h` and adds a public `ParsePubkey()` overload that returns the providers produced by the existing parser.

Key changes
- public overload uses P2TR key rules, permitting compressed, x-only, extended, and MuSig key expressions while rejecting uncompressed keys.
- Add `GetOriginInfo()` for retrieving explicitly provided key origin information.

---
Also, while I'm here, I noticed that `musig` parser accepted trailing characters apart from `/`. 
- Add a fix & test to reject unexpected trailing characters after a `musig()` expression

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). (You can use [this branch ](https://github.com/stratospher/bitcoin/commits/addrinfo_service_display/)to check the % of v2 addresses in a node's addrman.)

EDIT: see [summary](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30951#issuecomment-4346061700) on pros and cons for whether to allow v2 inbounds or not for `-v2onlyclearnet`.

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.

pulls.title: [32.x] Backports
wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author changes from `bad_function_call` to `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration to fail.

The second commit moves the check for an empty `mapWallet` to after `RunWithinTxn()` commits the database transaction and runs the commit callback, when transactions marked for removal have been deleted.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: refactor: pass BlockManager to ChainstateManager
pulls.body:
`ChainstateManager` creates and owns its `BlockManager`, which means block storage can't exist without chainstate management. #35627 discussed moving that ownership out of `ChainstateManager`, and the kernel needs it to configure, read and prune block storage on its own.

`NodeContext` and the kernel now create the `BlockManager` first, pass it to `ChainstateManager` by reference and destroy `ChainstateManager` first.

The first commit makes the kernel's `ChainMan` destroy its `ChainstateManager` explicitly. On master `ChainMan` declares its context last, which destroys the context before the `ChainstateManager` that refers into it. Nothing reads through those references during teardown, so this changes no behavior, but the order no longer depends on how the members are declared.

The last commit removes `ChainstateLoadOptions::prune`. It duplicated the `BlockManager`'s prune mode, and the kernel never set it. Once the kernel can prune (#36856), that would make it refuse to reopen a data directory it had pruned.

The only behavior change to my knowledge is startup log order, because the block tree database opens before the script verification threads start.

An earlier version of this PR also moved `ImportBlocks` and replaced `BlockManager`'s friend declarations. I've taken them out as they're not relevant to this, but I think together better suited for a change that removes the `node/blockstorage -> validation` circular dependency (#36858)

The kernel side is #36854.

pulls.title: wallet: Store information about created and imported multipath descriptors
pulls.body:
The wallet does not store any information about multipath descriptors. When a multipath descriptor is imported, it is first expanded, then the expansion descriptors are imported into the wallet.

This PR adds a field to `WalletDescriptor` which stores the IDs of the ScriptPubKeyMans of the descriptors that are part of the expansion, in the order that they are expanded. This allows us to use `ReconstructMultipath` to produce the multipath descriptor when necessary.

This is useful for working with hardware wallets that require policy registration, particularly those that require resending the descriptor that was registered.

`listdescriptors` is updated to include a `multipath_descriptor` field which contains the multipath descriptor for each individual descriptor if it originally came from a multipath descriptor.

Lastly, the automatically generated descriptors are now produced and stored as multipath descriptors, so `listdescriptors` will provide a `multipath_descriptor` for everything that the wallet automatically generates.

Note that the IDs stored in the wallet are ScriptPubKeyMan IDs, which we cannot compute from a descriptor as we assume to be opaque blobs since #35445.

Alternative to #36133, depends on #36442 and #36443

pulls.title: descriptor: Reconstruct a multipath descriptor from its expansion
pulls.body:
#36442 allows multipath descriptors to be represented in a single `Descriptor` object. `GetMultipathExpansion` returns the multiple descriptors represented by a multipath descriptor. This expansion is reversible - given the expansion in the order of the multipath elements, it is possible to determine what the original multipath descriptor was. This PR adds `ReconstructMultipath` to produce a new `Descriptor` representing the multipath descriptor that produced the expansion.

Depends on #36442

pulls.body:
Before eae193e750235e4023b3e6313284eede2cd7a022, Connect() only started the connection and returned true. If tor wasn't running the refusal was reported later and only logged under -debug=tor. Since eae193e750 (in v32), every failed reconnect attempt logs:

```

2026-11-04T14:14:08Z [warning] tor: Initiating connection to Tor control port 127.0.0.1:9051 failed
```

On a default configured node without tor, this pollutes debug.log with 18 lines every hour.

This improves it

pulls.title: descriptor: Represent multipath descriptors in a single Descriptor object
pulls.body:
Currently, multipath descriptor strings treat the multipath specifiers as syntactic sugar. Once we finish parsing such a string, the multipath elements are lost as the result is the multiple distinct descriptors that the multipath is a shorthand for. This means that we are unable to return the multipath string for such descriptors.

This PR allows descriptors to actually be multipath where the multipath specifiers are represented inside of the paths of `BIP32PubkeyProvider`s. This allows for the multipath string to be produced.

In order to achieve this, a lot of derivation path parsing is refactored. `KeyPath` is promoted to being its own class (which subclasses `std::vector`), while the individual derivation indexes become a `KeyPathElement` object so that the multipath elements can be represented. Furthermore, hardened derivation characters are now being stored within `KeyPathElement`s so each element knows what the original hardened character was. This also cleans up a little bit of the descriptor implementation as we no longer have to carry around `bool apostrophe` in a bunch of places.

Lastly, `Parse` now returns a single `Descriptor` object, rather than a vector of them. If the descriptor is a multipath descriptor, the expansion can be retrieved using `GetMultipathExpansion()`. The wallet uses this and still must not store multipath descriptors.

pulls.title: consensus: Remove special treatment for single threaded script checking
pulls.body:
This topic has been motivated by my work on batch validation and a related conversation just happened here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32467#discussion_r2098305199 

`CheckInputScripts` currently only does what its name implies if there is no multithreading usage for validation. If there are worker threads available the function instead only creates the checks and puts them into a vector. Aside from some shared pre-checks the multithreaded code path is much simpler compared to the rest. This dual use makes the function hard to grasp and its naming confusing.

This PR refactors this code to be more readable and improves documentation aside from unifying the single threaded and the multithreaded cases by letting checkqueue handle single threaded script checking as well. The code is already suited for this and there seems to be not noticable performance overhead from this.

pulls.title: p2p: Track recent stale tips (BIP 332)(Stale Tip Relay)

Part of #36833

This PR adds local tracking of recent stale tips for [BIP 332](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0332.md).
The feature is behind a new `-staletips=<mode>` option (default `none`). There is no P2P change yet: with `-staletips=headers` the node only tracks tips.

* A new `AcceptedStaleTip` validation notification feeds the staletips tracker.
* The tracker is built from the block index at startup, keeping the tips with the most work.

* `getchaintips` RPC updates

  * Report `fork_point` for each non-active tip.

Test networks get the stricter policies the BIP recommends:
* **signet:** only tips whose block has been validated, and one header variant per block. 
* **testnet3/4:** only tips with a difficulty of at least about 1,000,000.

pulls.title: wallet: allow skipping script paths
pulls.body:
While testing MuSig2 integration in #29675 I ran into a Ledger bug https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin-new/issues/329 that was triggered because we signed for a script path in addition to the key path. The bug itself will be fixed, but it seems useful in general to be able to skip script path signing (and finalizing).

For example, you may have a 2-of-2 musig() descriptor with some sort of fallback after coins are N blocks old. For both on chain privacy and fee reasons, you don't want to use this path unless absolutely necessary. But our wallet can't know if our co-signer still has their key, so we sign the script path at all times. This could lead to accidental broadcast.

This PR introduces a `keypath_only` option (default `false` for now) to the following RPC methods:
- `send` 
- `sendall`
- `walletcreatefundedpsbt`
- `walletprocesspsbt`
- `descriptorprocesspsbt`

The resulting PSBT won't _add_ `taproot_scripts` or `taproot_script_path_sigs`. It does still have `taproot_bip32_derivs` and `musig2_participant_pubkeys`.

It will not remove `taproot_scripts` from an existing PSBT, but it won't add a corresponding entry to `taproot_script_path_sigs`. We also won't finalize a PSBT without keypath spend, even with complete script paths. This protects against other participants accidentally including them.

The `wallet_taproot.py` tests are expanded to cover this behavior.

It can also be tested with https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc, gui: Allow users to manually rebroadcast a wallet transaction
pulls.body: From the discussion in #36403, it is clear that there needs to be a way for users to rebroadcast a transaction. Currently, the way to do so requires getting the raw transaction, getting the hex, and using `sendrawtransaction`. This PR adds `rebroadcastwallettx` RPC that takes a txid to attempt to rebroadcast that single transaction. An action is also added to the GUI menu for each transaction to do the same.

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric options were read with GetArg<int>() and then stored into unsigned or wider members without a range check. A negative value wrapped to a huge value and disabled the limit it was meant to configure, and a value wider than the destination could silently become a different number.

Parse the options whose destination is unsigned with ToIntegral<T>() on the raw string rather than with GetArg<T>(): the typed getter saturates values it cannot represent (so a leading '-' for an unsigned T becomes 0), while ToIntegral rejects '-', trailing garbage and overflow instead of saturating. Reject the remaining out-of-range values where they are read:

- -maxtipage: uint32_t seconds, range [0, UINT32_MAX]. A negative age placed the IBD cutoff in the future, so the node never treated its tip as recent.
- -dbbatchsize: uint64_t bytes. A negative value wrapped to a huge batch size and disabled flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch.
- -dbcrashratio: uint32_t, range [0, UINT32_MAX]. CoinsViewOptions::simulate_crash_ratio is changed from int to uint32_t to match.
- -limitclustercount: [1, MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT_LIMIT]. The separate upper-bound check in ApplyArgsManOptions is folded into this one, so an invalid value is reported once with one message.
- -limitclustersize: [1, INT64_MAX / 1000] kB. Zero made every transaction exceed the cluster size and blocked all mempool admission.
- -limitancestorcount, -limitdescendantcount: non-negative.
- -mempoolexpiry: [0, std::chrono::seconds::max() / 3600] hours, and the value is stored as seconds directly. The bound is taken from seconds rather than hours because std::chrono::hours is not guaranteed to be 64-bit.
- -datacarriersize: [0, UINT_MAX]; still unchecked when -datacarrier=0 turns the limit off.
- -bytespersigop: [0, UINT_MAX]. A negative value wrapped and inflated the sigop-adjusted size of every transaction until all were non-standard.
- -maxsendbuffer, -maxreceivebuffer: [0, UINT_MAX / 1000], since both are multiplied by 1000 into unsigned int members.
- -bantime: greater than 0. Zero or negative made setban without an explicit duration create an already expired ban.
- -timeout: positive and at most INT_MAX milliseconds. A non-positive value now fails instead of silently falling back to the default (as -peertimeout already did), and a value above INT_MAX used to narrow before it could be checked (e.g. 2^32 + 1 became 1).
- -txconfirmtarget: [1, UINT_MAX] in parameter interaction, and additionally bounded by the fee estimator's maximum when a wallet is loaded. A target beyond the estimator's range made every transaction fall back to -fallbackfee. The help text now states the minimum.

Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": -dbbatchsize, -datacarriersize, -mempoolexpiry, -maxtipage, -bytespersigop, -maxsendbuffer, -maxreceivebuffer, -limitancestorcount and -limitdescendantcount.

Since -nofoo is parsed as 0, add DISALLOW_NEGATION to the options where 0 is valid but very different from "no limit": -dbbatchsize, -mempoolexpiry, -maxreceivebuffer, -maxsendbuffer, -maxtipage, -limitancestorcount, -limitdescendantcount and -datacarriersize. Options that already reject (-bantime, -timeout, -peertimeout, -limitclustercount, -limitclustersize, -txconfirmtarget) need no separate check: negation reports the value error once. -bytespersigop still allows negation, because 0 turns the sigop adjustment off, which is exactly what -nobytespersigop says.

ReadCoinsViewArgs now returns util::Result<void> (marked [[nodiscard]]) so its errors abort startup instead of being discarded.

Finally, -help gains the =<n> placeholder for the options that take a value (-dbbatchsize, -bytespersigop, -datacarriersize, -stopatheight, -checkblockindex) and states the bounds for -bantime, -limitclustercount, -limitclustersize and -txconfirmtarget.

Add unit tests for the option parsers and functional tests for the accepted, rejected and negated forms.

pulls.body: Because `nodes[1]` time was not mocked in test_block_inv, it was possible for wall clock to advance 2s by the time `nodes[0]` had delivered a tx announcement to it. Then, `nodes[1]` would request the tx from a test peer, never receive the tx, and fail in sync_mempools().

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: guix: backport oscrypto PBKDF2 timing fix
pulls.body:
With substitutes disabled, `guix-codesign` can fail when building [oscrypto](https://pypi.org/project/oscrypto/) 1.3.0. The `test_dump_private` test raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

The Guix time-machine bump in bitcoin/bitcoin#36233 (merged after the 32.x branch-off) pulls in OpenSSL 3.5.5, which can finish oscrypto's initial PBKDF2 benchmark in under a millisecond. oscrypto truncates this duration to zero and then divides by it. This was fixed upstream in wbond/oscrypto@144c12195001b08b9ccecb8a3fd041d22ae24474

This PR adds the fix to `contrib/guix/patches`. It can be dropped once a new oscrypto release includes the fix and a Guix time machine bump includes it.

pulls.title: test: [NOMERGE,SKETCH] Add thread-safe fast-failing test macros
pulls.body:
Currently, the unit tests use different boost check macros. However, this is problematic:

* The check macros are tied to the boost test framework and can not be used in other tests, such as the fuzz tests.
* The check macros are not overflow-safe. For example `BOOST_CHECK_GT(-10, 10U);` compiles and passes fine, even though it is obviously wrong.
* The check macros are not thread-safe. Using them in a thread will compile fine, but then fail tsan later on. Usually it is trivial to replace them by a plain `assert`, but it would be better if the macros just worked under tsan.
* The check macros are not fast-failing. This is confusing, as the test continues to run and will print more logs, making it harder to spot the first failure. Also, it is contrary to the internal check macros `assert` and `Assert`, and even `CHECK_NONFATAL` under debug mode, which all lead to an immediate abort.

Fix all issues by adding new check macros: `ASSERT`, `ASSERT_EQ` (and friends), `ASSERT_EQ_COLLECTIONS` (C++20 range-based), as well as `ASSERT_EXCEPTION`. They can be used as a drop-in replacement for the corresponding boost macro.

The implementation for all macros is only ~150 LOC, so it should be preferable to any external dependency addressing the above issues (which I couldn't find anyway).

(Tracking issue: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34666)

### Note on naming (why `ASSERT`?)

The test macros follow the naming and semantics of the internal Bitcoin Core macros (`assert`, and `Assert`). While it may confusing to have three unary `assert` macros that do *roughly* the same, it should be harmless and any macro that compiles is fine to use. (There is a special edge case to `Assert`, which allows to be turned into an exception as part of `g_detail_test_only_CheckFailuresAreExceptionsNotAborts`, but this shouldn't matter much).

In theory, if devs didn't care about nice diagnostic messages on a failure (printing the left and right side), the macros could even be a direct alias of `assert` or `Assert`, reducing the LOC even more. Though, I think it is fine and preferable to have slightly better failure messages in tests.

Also, the naming and semantics follow the Bitcoin Core functional test macros, which also start with `assert_`.

### Later optimizations

The macros are currently sitting in the header, but once they are applied to the whole codebase, the pretty-printing implementation can move to a cpp file, which reduces the weight of the header and makes it possible to change or add pretty-printing features without a whole re-compilation of all tests.

pulls.title: wallet: relax external_signer flag constraints
pulls.body:
The `external_signer` indicates that an external signer device may be called via [HWI](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI) or [equivalent](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/external-signer.md#signer-api) application.

When it was initially introduced some additional constraints were placed on wallets with this flag: it had to be a descriptor wallet and watch-only. Also the flag could not be added or removed later.

The constraints aren't a problem for the main supported and documented use case of connecting a single hardware wallet and using it just like a normal single sig Bitcoin Core wallet.

But they get in the way of MuSig2 support, see https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

This pull request drops the following constraints:

- `disable_private_keys` is no longer mandatory (but still default)
- `external_signer` flag is now mutable

Changing the `external_signer` flag reloads the wallet so that its descriptor ScriptPubKeyMans are recreated using the new setting.

Additionally it does the following:

- make the `blank` option for `createwallet` consistent with regular wallets by _not_ importing keys from the connected signer
- avoid going through `createTransaction` for external signers (otherwise the GUI breaks)
- create an `ExternalSignerScriptPubKeyMan` when importing a descriptor into an external signer wallet, instead of requiring an additional reload

This should have no noticeable effect on the default single sig use case described above.

Finally we add test coverage for spending from an imported hot key descriptor in an external signer wallet. The wallet signs with its own keys before involving the external signer.

pulls.title: wallet/feebumper: reject an `original_change_index` output without a destination
pulls.body:
Moved from #35302 due to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35302#issuecomment-7126751401.

This PR:
- refactors `CreateRateBumpTransaction` to return a `util::Expected` of a Result and Error Struct instead of using out params.  This change makes it easier for #35302 to add a sp_recipients field to the Result Struct instead of adding a new output parameter.
- rejects an `original_change_index` that specifies an output without a destination. The pre-existing behaviour silently replaced the specified output if an `OP_RETURN` output was specified.

pulls.title: streams: handle buffered write failures outside the destructor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block and undo writers rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the last buffered bytes.
If the filesystem fills up, `fwrite()` can write fewer bytes than requested (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
When this happens during the final flush, `AutoFile::write_buffer()` throws and the exception escapes the implicitly non-throwing destructor, invoking `std::terminate` before the node can report the write error and shut down normally.
Adding an explicit `flush()` alone would still leave the same bytes pending on failure, so the destructor would retry the write during unwinding.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly. If serialization or flushing throws `std::ios_base::failure`, they call `discard()` to drop any pending bytes, log the error, close the file, and request shutdown.

`BufferedWriter::flush()` clears the pending byte count before calling `write_buffer()` and propagates any exception. Retrying would be unsafe because the stream may have obfuscated the bytes in place and a short write may already have put some of them on disk.
The destructor uses `Assume` to check that no bytes are pending before its fallback flush.

<details>
<summary>Manual write-error reproducer</summary>

Force `AutoFile::write_buffer()` to report a write failure even when `fwrite()` succeeds.

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, flushing from the destructor invokes `std::terminate`.

```text
libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::__1::ios_base::failure: AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
zsh: abort      build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"
exit=134
```

With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure, completes normal shutdown, and exits with status 1.

```text
Checking all blk files are present...
[error] Failed to write block file FlatFilePos(nFile=0, nPos=8): AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
...
Error: A fatal internal error occurred, see debug.log for details: Failed to write block.
[error] Writing genesis block to disk failed
[error] Error initializing block database
...
Shutdown done
exit=1
```
</details>

pulls.title: blocks: add resumable reobfuscation for existing block files
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Nodes that synced before v28 may store block and undo files effectively unobfuscated with a zero XOR key. There is no built-in way to obfuscate those existing files, rotate their key, or deliberately replace it with a zero key without resyncing.

**Fix:** Add `-reobfuscate-blocks[=<value>]` to rewrite existing `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files before chainstate loading. With no value or `=1`, the option generates a random 8-byte key. A 16-character hexadecimal value selects an exact key, including all zeros to remove obfuscation, while malformed values fail during startup. If the selected key is already active, block and undo files are left unchanged.

Files are rewritten in fixed-size chunks, staged with a `.reobfuscated` suffix, committed before the originals are removed, and renamed to their original names after all rewrites finish. The target key is staged as `xor.dat.reobfuscated`, which is also used to resume an interrupted migration. Progress is reported in the log and through kernel notifications marked as resumable.

**Benchmark:** The migration is single-threaded and processes one file at a time.

| CPU | Storage | Block count | Size | Files | Time (min) | Blocks/min |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Apple M4 Max laptop | SSD | ~955k | ~854 GB | 11,232 | 10.18 | 93,804 |
| Intel Core i9 | SSD | ~909k | ~725 GB | 10,238 | 23.1 | 39,351 |
| Raspberry Pi 5 | SSD | ~914k | ~728 GB | 10,276 | 72.78 | 12,558 |
| Intel Core i7 | HDD | ~909k | ~720 GB | 10,156 | 208.7 | 4,356 |
| Raspberry Pi 4B | HDD | ~915k | ~730 GB | 10,304 | 1467 | 624 |

**Similar work:**

- [contrib: add xor-blocks tool to obfuscate blocks directory #32451](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32451)
- [andrewtoth/blocks-xor](https://github.com/andrewtoth/blocks-xor)

pulls.title: validation: reduce block index comparison overhead
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block index ordering is used by chain selection and `CheckBlockIndex()`. The work comparator is defined out of line and can compare the same chain work twice.
`CheckBlockIndex()` is enabled by default on regtest, including functional tests, but disabled by default on mainnet.

**Fix:** Inline the block-index comparators, compare the work-ordering key with `std::tie`, and use one three-way comparison per 32-bit word in `arith_uint256`.

| Compiler     | Synthetic 256-bit work comparisons | CheckBlockIndex |
|--------------|-----------------------------------:|----------------:|
| GCC 15.0.1   |                              6.51× |           1.62× |
| Clang 22.0.0 |                              6.80× |           1.39× |

pulls.title: sign: add musig2 data after validating musig2 involvement
pulls.body:
Previously, signing was assuming that MuSig2 information from the given `SigningProvider` was all from the descriptor that is relevant to the input being signed. However, in both `descriptorprocesspsbt` and `utxoupdatepsbt`, this is not true as information from all provided descriptors is put into the `SigningProvider` that is passed to `SignTaproot`. Consequently, if one of the given descriptors involved a MuSig2, the MuSig2 information would be accidentally added to the `SignatureData` which results in those fields appearing in the resulting PSBT.

Both the filling of aggregate pubkey information as well as participant BIP 32 derivation paths is moved to after the aggregate pubkey check inside of `SignMuSig2`. This ensures that information about only the aggregates pertaining to the particular script being signed are included in the resulting PSBT.

Fixes #36323

pulls.title: build: Bump g++ minimum supported version to 13
pulls.body:
At some point, it may be fine to [drop support for older vanilla systems](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979) not shipping with at least GCC 13.

(For this bump, only C++20 `std::format` will become available, but this bump should also pave the way for C++23.)

This patch will only be released in version 33.x, or later, next year (2027).

For reference:

* https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/g++ (g++-13)
* https://packages.debian.org/trixie/g++ (g++-14)
* CentOS-like 8/9/10 ship recent GCC via appstream (`dnf install -y gcc-toolset-15`)
* Free/Open/Net*BSD ship a recent GCC
* OpenSuse Leap and Tumbleweed ship with g++ 15 https://software.opensuse.org/package/gcc15-c++

On operating systems where the minimum GCC version is not shipped by default, the user would have to use Clang, or install GCC in a different way. For example:

* Debian Bookworm could use https://packages.debian.org/bookworm/clang-22
* Ubuntu 22.04 would have to use a general alternative:
* [PPA](https://launchpad.net/~ubuntu-toolchain-r/+archive/ubuntu/test), https://apt.llvm.org/ (for Clang), brew, nix, guix, or compile GCC from source, ...

Obviously, downloading pre-compiled releases or compiling previous release branches is unaffected by this change.
